extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, peer reviewers, and scholars interested in the ethics and methodology of peer review (especially in psychology and related sciences)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for designing, evaluating, and ethically justifying empirical studies of the peer‑review process and for improving peer‑review practices; includes methodological, ethical, and editorial considerations. Geared to scholarly research and editorial policy discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and evaluation of competing hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Good research design consists of identifying the most plausible alternative explanations (rival hypotheses) for an observed finding and evaluating their validity; if rival hypotheses are not supported, the original claim becomes more credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much of the target study's strength was that Peters & Ceci (P & C) identified and assessed seemingly reasonable rival explanations and demonstrated their implausibility; many contending explanations and evidence against them are summarized (see Table 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain written permission from original authors and publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Permission should be obtained in writing from original authors and from publishers before using previously published papers as test manuscripts or otherwise manipulating submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C obtained written permission from all but one senior author and from eight non-APA publishers; this is presented as a commendable ethical/procedural feature (exception due to clerical mistake noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select important and engaging research questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The questions raised by the study should command interest and, where appropriate, be daring (e.g., investigating detection of previously published work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary notes that P & C's questions command much interest and that the detection question could be labeled daring, implying importance/novelty is a criterion for study design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent discussion of the study's importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should competently discuss why the study matters and situate its contribution to knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C's article is praised for a competent discussion of its importance; such discussion helps justify methodological choices (see item 3 of commendable features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough documentation of claims and contrary findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about the reviewing process and previous research must be amply documented, and contrary findings should be reported rather than omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The target article documented claims about the reviewing process and previous research and reported contrary findings (item 4). Thorough documentation increases credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural/realistic settings (ecological validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible, conduct investigations in a natural setting to preserve ecological validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C used a natural setting for their study (item 5), which is highlighted as commendable for studies of peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear rationale for manipulated independent variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulating variables (e.g., author/institution prestige), present a good rationale explaining why the manipulated factor is important to the phenomenon under study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C provided rationale for why the manipulable independent variable (prestige) mattered (item 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Full transparency in describing journals, articles, institutions, and treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the journals, the articles used, author institutions, and precisely what the treatment/intervention was so readers understand context and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C described journals, articles, and author institutions and clearly told the reader what the treatment was (item 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and validate operational measures (e.g., 'prestige')
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide evidence to document how key constructs (like prestige or affiliation status) are operationalized and validated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C presented evidence to document 'prestige' affiliation (item 8); measurement validation strengthens claims about effects of such constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against superficial detection while preserving meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: When attempting to blind or mask manuscripts, guard against reviewers detecting the manipulation via superficial cues, but do so without changing manuscript meaning or compromising the treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C were commended for guarding against superficial detection of papers without changing meaning or compromising the treatment (item 9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate time lag between original publication and resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a time lag that balances the chance reviewers could have read the original (so detection is reasonable) against being so short that reviewers would not have had time to read the articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C used an 18–32 month lag (item 10) and justify it as short enough to expect detection but long enough for reviewers to have had a chance to read the articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a plausible mechanism or description of causal process
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond empirical association, offer a plausible explanation or description of the mechanism by which a variable (e.g., prestige) affects outcomes (e.g., acceptance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C provided a description of the mechanism of why prestige mattered (item 11), improving interpretability of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present convergent evidence and triangulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Support primary findings with convergent evidence from other observations or analyses (e.g., reviewer agreement patterns across blinded vs nonblinded journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C presented convergent evidence (item 12): observed greater reviewer agreement for nonblind journals was added to the major premise supporting reviewer-bias hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag conjectures and speculative claims explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Call readers' attention to conjectures or speculative elements rather than presenting them as established facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C's conjectures were explicitly called to readers' attention (item 13). Explicit labeling of speculation aids honest interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge study limitations and implications; offer suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out limitations of the study (even if only some are mentioned), note implications of findings, and suggest concrete steps or policy implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C pointed out some limitations (item 14) and noted implications and suggestions (item 15). Commentaries urge follow-up steps to reduce peer-review abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh benefits against costs (ethical balancing) per professional codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess ethically contentious research (e.g., deception) by balancing potential benefits to knowledge against possible costs to participants and others, in accordance with professional ethical codes (e.g., APA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA Code (1973) is cited: whether research is ethically reprehensible, acceptable, or praiseworthy depends on considered judgment weighing benefits and costs (Mindick). This must be done case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize harm and burden to research subjects (reviewers/editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize imposition on the time, energy, and reputational discomfort of reviewers and editors who are research subjects, especially when participation is voluntary and uncompensated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary notes costs of P & C's deception research included time/energy imposition and potential embarrassment; such harms should be minimized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify ethically problematic methods by clear metascientific benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: If using ethically sensitive methods (e.g., deception), provide strong justification by demonstrating substantial metascientific benefits and potential to inform corrective actions that obviate future need for deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P & C's study is portrayed as metascientific and potentially valuable for understanding how knowledge becomes property of scientists; benefits may justify the ethical costs if they lead to steps minimizing peer-review abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and report the subjective/aesthetic elements of scientific work
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that taste, style, judgment, and aesthetics influence evaluations; consider ways to let scientists disclose subjective aspects so work can be judged in full context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitroff suggests reporting both 'objective' methods and a parallel stream‑of‑consciousness account of thoughts/feelings during research, arguing that acknowledging subjectivity may improve evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider disciplinary differences when generalizing peer-review findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for field-specific features — rejection rates, consensus and cumulativeness, subfield delineation, resource intensity, preprint culture and communication networks — when extrapolating findings across disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moravcsik lists five reasons physics might differ (lower rejection rates, well-delineated subfields, resource needs, faster outdating, strong preprint/grapevine), illustrating the need to consider such differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use blinded review to reduce identity-based bias where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Blinded (anonymous) reviewing reduces bias arising from knowledge of author identity or affiliation and helps prevent prejudice against unknown authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nelson notes her positive experience with blind reviewing at Developmental Psychology and explains how masking author identity reduces bias; caveat: sometimes identities are guessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find alternative bias-reduction methods where blinding is infeasible (e.g., grant review)
rubrics_metrics.description: When blinded review is not possible (e.g., grant proposals where investigator competence must be assessed), seek alternative solutions and maintain vigilance against bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nelson highlights that grant proposals cannot be blind and suggests alternative approaches are needed to control for bias in those contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine editorial selection and decision processes as potential bias sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate editors' practices (who they send manuscripts to, how they weight reviewers' recommendations) because editorial selective practices may produce bias independent of individual reviewers' criteria shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over argues that identity/status may determine reviewer selection and editorial action; bias might reflect editors' selective practices rather than reviewers changing acceptance criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze reviewer behavior using signal detection concepts (discriminability vs criterion shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame reviewer decisions analytically: bias may reflect changes in discriminability (attention to defects for low-status authors) or criterion shifts (different acceptance thresholds), and distinguishing these is important for interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over and others suggest conceptualizing results as discriminability rather than pure criterion effects; reviewers may attend more to flaws for low-status authors (discriminability) rather than uniformly applying defects (criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to both false negatives and false positives in editorial outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider both types of errors: false negatives (publishable work rejected) and false positives (unacceptable manuscripts published); focusing only on one mischaracterizes quality issues in publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nelson remarks that P & C focused on false negatives but the study could equally focus on false positives; the publication ecosystem and incentives (publish-or-perish) can raise the rate of publishable-but-trivial work.
